Global Development Analytics & Predictive Decision System¶

Analyzing and Predicting GDP per Capita Using SQL, Python & Machine Learning¶

Project Overview¶

This project analyzes country-level development patterns using selected indicators from the World Development Indicators (WDI) dataset.

The objective is to understand how economic, demographic, digital, labour-market and trade-related indicators are associated with GDP per capita, and to examine whether information from the previous year can be used to predict GDP per capita in the following year.

The project combines exploratory analysis, statistical analysis and machine learning to move from understanding historical development patterns to evaluating predictive performance.

Project Journey¶

World Bank → DataHub → Excel → MySQL / SQL → Python → Statistical Analysis → Machine Learning → Prediction Gap Analysis → Decision Support

Analysis Period¶

2010–2024

Unit of Analysis¶

Each observation represents a country-year, meaning one country or economy measured during one specific year.

World Bank regional, income-group and other aggregate entities are excluded from the country-level predictive analysis.

Target Variable¶

GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)

Development Indicators¶

  1. Population Growth
  2. Life Expectancy
  3. Internet Usage
  4. Unemployment
  5. Exports as % of GDP

Predictive Question¶

Can previous-year GDP per capita and historical development indicators be used to predict a country's GDP per capita in the following year?

Predictive Approach¶

The project compares:

  • Naive Baseline — previous-year GDP only
  • Indicators-Only Models — five previous-year development indicators
  • Full Models — previous-year GDP combined with the five development indicators

Signature Analysis¶

Global Development Progression Funnel

Observe → Explain → Predict → Diagnose → Support Decisions

Business Problem & Analytical Questions¶

Business Problem¶

Countries differ considerably in their economic and development conditions. Understanding how development indicators are associated with GDP per capita can help identify broader development patterns.

This project also examines whether historical information can provide useful predictions of GDP per capita for the following year.

The analysis therefore addresses both descriptive and predictive questions rather than relying only on model performance.

Analytical Questions¶

  • How does GDP per capita vary across countries and years?
  • How are population growth, life expectancy, internet usage, unemployment and exports as a percentage of GDP associated with GDP per capita?
  • Which development indicators show stronger statistical relationships with GDP per capita?
  • Can the five development indicators from the previous year predict GDP per capita in the following year?
  • How does an indicators-only model compare with a simple previous-year GDP baseline?
  • How does predictive performance change when previous-year GDP is added to the development indicators?
  • Where are the larger differences between predicted and actual GDP per capita?

Analytical Approach¶

EDA → Statistical Analysis → Next-Year Prediction → Model Comparison → Prediction Gap Analysis → Decision Support

The predictive analysis uses a time-based train–test approach, with earlier observations used for training and later observations from 2023–2024 used for testing.

The analysis identifies statistical relationships and predictive patterns. It does not claim that the selected indicators directly cause changes in GDP per capita or represent official economic forecasts.

Dataset & Variable Definitions¶

Country¶

Country_Name identifies the country or economy represented by each observation.

Country_Code provides the corresponding country/economy code.

For the country-level predictive analysis, World Bank regional, income-group and other aggregate entities are excluded.

Year¶

Year identifies the year in which the development indicators were measured.

Each row represents a country-year observation.

Target Variable — GDP per Capita¶

GDP_per_capita

GDP per capita represents GDP divided by the population of the economy.

Measurement: Constant 2015 US dollars

The use of constant prices adjusts the series for price changes over time, allowing GDP per capita to be compared across years using 2015 prices.

Predictor 1 — Population Growth¶

Population_growth

Measures the annual percentage change in population.

Measurement: Percentage (%)

Predictor 2 — Life Expectancy¶

Life_expectancy

Measures the expected number of years a newborn would live under the mortality conditions prevailing at the time of measurement.

Measurement: Years

Predictor 3 — Internet Usage¶

Internet_usage

Measures the share of the population using the Internet.

Measurement: Percentage (%)

Predictor 4 — Unemployment¶

Unemployment

Measures unemployment as a share of the labour force.

Measurement: Percentage (%)

Predictor 5 — Exports as % of GDP¶

Exports_pct_GDP

Measures exports of goods and services relative to the size of the economy.

Measurement: Percentage of GDP (%)

Variable Summary¶

Variable Role Measurement
Country_Name Identifier Country
Country_Code Identifier Code
Year Time Year
GDP_per_capita Target Constant 2015 US$
Population_growth Predictor %
Life_expectancy Predictor Years
Internet_usage Predictor %

Data Journey & Technology Stack¶

Data Journey¶

The dataset was not taken directly into Python. It followed a multi-stage preparation and validation process:

World Bank WDI ↓
DataHub ↓
Excel — Data Preparation ↓
MySQL — Data Storage ↓
SQL — Data Validation ↓
Python — EDA & Statistical Analysis ↓
Country-Level Data Preparation ↓
Lagged Variables & Next-Year Prediction Dataset ↓
Machine Learning ↓
Prediction Gap Analysis ↓
Power BI — Decision Support

SQL Validation Completed Before Python¶

The dataset was validated in MySQL using:

  • Record counts
  • Country coverage
  • Year range using MIN() and MAX()
  • Missing-value checks
  • Duplicate checks
  • Basic value and range checks

Python therefore begins with the validated SQL dataset rather than repeating the complete SQL validation process.

Predictive Data Preparation¶

Before predictive modeling:

  • World Bank aggregate entities were removed.
  • Lagged variables were created using previous-year observations.
  • Non-consecutive year gaps were excluded from the lagged prediction data.
  • A time-based train–test split was used, with 2011–2022 for training and 2023–2024 for testing.

Technology Stack¶

**Excel | MySQL | SQL | Python | Pandas | NumPy | Matplotlib | Seaborn | SciPy | Scikit-learn | Power BI **

The analysis focuses on:

  • GDP per capita distribution
  • Predictor distributions
  • GDP per capita across countries
  • Relationships between GDP per capita and the five predictors
  • Correlation between variables
  • Development trends over time

EDA Insights¶

The exploratory analysis helps identify the major patterns in the dataset before moving into statistical analysis and predictive modeling.

Key Observations¶

  • GDP per capita shows substantial variation across country-year observations.
  • The five development indicators also show considerable variation across economies.
  • The scatter plots provide an initial view of the relationships between GDP per capita and each predictor.
  • The correlation matrix helps identify the strength and direction of linear relationships between the variables.
  • The time-series analysis shows how average development indicators have changed during the 2010–2024 period.

These observations provide the basis for the next stage of analysis: statistical testing and regression analysis.

Important: These are exploratory relationships. Correlation or association does not establish causation.

Statistical Analysis — Pearson Correlation¶

Pearson correlation is used to measure the strength and direction of the linear relationship between GDP per capita and each of the five development indicators.

How it helps this project: It provides an initial statistical understanding of which development indicators are more strongly associated with GDP per capita, helping us interpret the relationships before moving into multiple regression and predictive modeling.

The analysis reports:

  • Pearson correlation coefficient (r) — strength and direction of the relationship.
  • p-value — statistical significance of the observed relationship.

Important: Correlation shows association, not causation.

In [11]:
# ============================================================
#   PEARSON CORRELATION & SIGNIFICANCE TEST
# ============================================================

predictors = [
    "Population_growth",
    "Life_expectancy",
    "Internet_usage",
    "Unemployment",
    "Exports_pct_GDP"
]

correlation_results = []

for predictor in predictors:
    
    temp = df[["GDP_per_capita", predictor]].dropna()
    
    r, p_value = stats.pearsonr(
        temp["GDP_per_capita"],
        temp[predictor]
    )
    
    correlation_results.append({
        "Predictor": predictor,
        "Pearson_r": r,
        "p_value": p_value
    })

correlation_results = pd.DataFrame(correlation_results)

correlation_results["Relationship"] = np.where(
    correlation_results["Pearson_r"] > 0,
    "Positive",
    "Negative"
)

correlation_results["Significant_at_5pct"] = np.where(
    correlation_results["p_value"] < 0.05,
    "Yes",
    "No"
)

correlation_results.sort_values(
    by="Pearson_r",
    ascending=False
)

Statistical Analysis — Multiple Linear Regression¶

Multiple Linear Regression is used to examine the combined relationship between GDP per capita and the five selected development indicators.

This analysis provides a statistical benchmark before moving to the next-year predictive modeling stage.

In [12]:
# ============================================================
#   MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION
# ============================================================

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error

regression_columns = [
    "GDP_per_capita",
    "Population_growth",
    "Life_expectancy",
    "Internet_usage",
    "Unemployment",
    "Exports_pct_GDP"
]

regression_df = df[regression_columns].dropna()

X = regression_df[
    [
        "Population_growth",
        "Life_expectancy",
        "Internet_usage",
        "Unemployment",
        "Exports_pct_GDP"
    ]
]

y = regression_df["GDP_per_capita"]

# Fit multiple linear regression
linear_model = LinearRegression()
linear_model.fit(X, y)

# Predictions
y_pred = linear_model.predict(X)

# Model performance
r2 = r2_score(y, y_pred)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y, y_pred)
rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y, y_pred))

# Coefficients
coefficients = pd.DataFrame({
    "Predictor": X.columns,
    "Coefficient": linear_model.coef_
})

print("Multiple Linear Regression Results")
print("=" * 50)

print(f"R² Score : {r2:.3f}")
print(f"MAE      : {mae:,.2f}")
print(f"RMSE     : {rmse:,.2f}")

print("\nRegression Coefficients:")
display(coefficients)

Predictive Modeling — Next-Year GDP Prediction¶

Prediction Approach¶

The predictive analysis is designed to answer the following question:

Given a country's economic and development conditions in one year, what GDP per capita would the model predict for the following year?

Instead of using indicators from the same year to predict that year's GDP per capita, the model uses previous-year information to predict the GDP per capita of the following year.

How the Historical Data Is Used¶

The dataset covers 2010–2024. Each year provides historical information that can be used to create a next-year prediction.

For example:

2010 indicators → Predict 2011 GDP per capita
2011 indicators → Predict 2012 GDP per capita
2022 indicators → Predict 2023 GDP per capita
2023 indicators → Predict 2024 GDP per capita

Therefore, the earlier years are not discarded. They provide the historical observations required for the model to learn development patterns over time.

Predictor Structure¶

For each country-year observation:

Previous-year GDP per capita

  • Previous-year Population Growth
  • Previous-year Life Expectancy
  • Previous-year Internet Usage
  • Previous-year Unemployment
  • Previous-year Exports as % of GDP

↓

Current-year GDP per capita

Time-Based Train–Test Split¶

A time-based train–test split is used because the objective is to predict future GDP per capita using information available from the past.

The model is trained using earlier years and evaluated using later, unseen years.

This preserves the chronological order of the data and prevents future observations from being used to train the model before they are evaluated.

Why This Approach?¶

This creates a realistic predictive workflow:

Historical Development Conditions → Next-Year GDP Prediction → Actual vs Predicted GDP → Prediction Gap Analysis

The actual GDP per capita values are kept unchanged. The model is evaluated based on how closely its predictions match the observed values.

World Bank Aggregate Filtering¶

The World Bank dataset contains both individual countries/economies and aggregate entities, such as regions, income groups and global totals.

For this project, the unit of analysis is the country-year observation. Therefore, aggregate entities were removed before creating lagged variables and building the predictive models.

This step ensures that the analysis focuses on individual country-level development patterns and prevents regional or income-group aggregates from being treated as individual countries.

Filtering the aggregates before lag creation is important because the lagged variables are calculated within each country. Keeping aggregate entities could otherwise introduce non-country observations into the predictive dataset.

After filtering, the dataset contains only the country/economy observations used for the subsequent next-year prediction analysis.

# ============================================================
# CREATE LAGGED VARIABLES FOR NEXT-YEAR PREDICTION
# ============================================================
# Lagged variables represent the previous year's values.
# A lag is kept only when the previous observation is exactly
# one calendar year earlier.

df = df.sort_values(["Country_Code", "Year"]).copy()

lag_columns = [
    "GDP_per_capita",
    "Population_growth",
    "Life_expectancy",
    "Internet_usage",
    "Unemployment",
    "Exports_pct_GDP"
]

# Create previous-observation lags
for col in lag_columns:
    df[f"{col}_lag1"] = df.groupby("Country_Code")[col].shift(1)

# Check whether the lag is exactly one calendar year earlier
df["Lag_Year"] = df.groupby("Country_Code")["Year"].shift(1)

invalid_mask = df["Lag_Year"].notna() & ((df["Year"] - df["Lag_Year"]) != 1)

# Remove non-consecutive lags
lagged_columns = [f"{col}_lag1" for col in lag_columns]
df.loc[invalid_mask, lagged_columns] = np.nan

print(f"Non-consecutive lag observations excluded: {invalid_mask.sum():,}")

# Remove helper column
df.drop(columns=["Lag_Year"], inplace=True)

Non-consecutive lag observations excluded: 10

    ["Country_Name", "Country_Code", "Year"] +

# ============================================================
# TRAIN / TEST SPLIT — TIME BASED
# ============================================================

train_df = model_df[model_df["Year"] <= 2022].copy()
test_df = model_df[model_df["Year"] >= 2023].copy()

X_train = train_df[model_features]
y_train = train_df[target]

X_test = test_df[model_features]
y_test = test_df[target]

print("Training data:", X_train.shape)

Key Findings & Implications¶

The analysis focused on two main questions: how the selected development indicators are related to GDP per capita, and how useful these indicators are for predicting GDP per capita one year ahead.

Key Findings¶

  • GDP per capita shows substantial variation across countries and years, reflecting differences in economic and development conditions.

  • The five selected indicators — population growth, life expectancy, internet usage, unemployment and exports as a percentage of GDP — show different levels of association with GDP per capita. These relationships describe statistical patterns and should not be interpreted as evidence of causation.

  • The predictive analysis uses information from the previous year to estimate GDP per capita for the following year. This time-based approach provides a more realistic evaluation than using information from the same year as the prediction target.

  • Three prediction approaches were compared: a naive baseline, indicators-only models, and full models that combine the five indicators with previous-year GDP per capita.

  • The naive baseline performed strongly, showing that previous-year GDP per capita contains substantial information about the following year's GDP.

  • The indicators-only models provide a clearer view of the predictive information contained in the five development indicators. Random Forest achieved an R² of approximately 0.83, compared with approximately 0.43 for Linear Regression.

  • The full models achieved much higher predictive performance after including previous-year GDP per capita. This result needs to be interpreted in context because GDP per capita tends to be persistent from one year to the next.

  • For India in 2024, the actual GDP per capita was $2,366.83. Linear Regression predicted $2,429.08, while Random Forest predicted $2,300.03. This demonstrates how the models can be used to compare predicted and observed values for a specific country-year.

Decision Support Perspective¶

The prediction stage is intended to provide an analytical benchmark rather than an official economic forecast. Comparing predicted GDP per capita with actual values helps identify observations where the model's estimate differs from the observed outcome.

The Prediction Gap Analysis highlights country-year observations with larger differences between predicted and actual GDP per capita. These observations can be examined further using additional economic, demographic, policy and country-specific information that is outside the scope of this project.

The comparison between indicators-only and full models is also important. It shows the predictive contribution of the five selected development indicators separately from the strong year-to-year persistence of GDP per capita.

Overall, the results indicate that the selected development indicators contain useful predictive information, but they are not sufficient on their own to predict GDP per capita with the same level of accuracy as models that also use previous-year GDP.

The results represent statistical relationships and analytical predictions, not causal explanations or official economic forecasts.

Limitations¶

  • The analysis focuses on five selected development indicators and therefore does not capture all economic, social, demographic and policy factors that may be associated with GDP per capita.

  • The full models include previous-year GDP per capita, which is highly persistent over time. Therefore, their strong predictive performance should not be interpreted as evidence that the five development indicators alone can predict GDP per capita with similar accuracy.

  • The indicators-only models provide a more direct assessment of the predictive information contained in the selected development indicators, but their performance is lower than that of the full models.

  • The prediction framework uses previous-year information to estimate the following year's GDP per capita. Unexpected events such as economic shocks, crises or policy changes during the prediction year are not captured by the selected predictors.

  • The dataset covers 2010–2024, so the findings are based on this historical period and may not necessarily apply to other periods.

  • Data availability varies across countries, resulting in different numbers of observations between economies.

  • The analysis identifies statistical relationships and predictive patterns but does not establish causal relationships between the development indicators and GDP per capita.

  • Prediction gaps indicate where model estimates differ from observed values, but the gap itself does not explain the underlying economic reasons for the difference.

  • The results should therefore be interpreted as analytical predictions and benchmarks rather than official economic forecasts.

Final Conclusion¶

This project developed an end-to-end Global Development Analytics & Predictive Decision System, beginning with World Bank data and progressing through Excel preparation, MySQL/SQL validation, Python-based exploratory analysis, statistical analysis and machine learning.

The analysis examined GDP per capita in relation to five development indicators: population growth, life expectancy, internet usage, unemployment and exports as a percentage of GDP.

For prediction, the project used a time-based train–test approach, training the models on historical observations from 2011–2022 and evaluating them on later, unseen observations from 2023–2024. This preserves the chronological structure of the data and provides a more realistic framework for next-year prediction.

Rather than relying on a single model score, the project compared three different prediction approaches:

  1. Naive Baseline — uses previous-year GDP per capita to predict the following year.
  2. Indicators-Only Models — use the five lagged development indicators without GDP per capita.
  3. Full Models — combine the five development indicators with previous-year GDP per capita.

The comparison shows that the five development indicators contain useful predictive information, particularly when modeled using Random Forest. At the same time, the strong performance of the full models and the naive baseline demonstrates the importance of GDP's year-to-year persistence.

The project also applied the analysis to India 2024 and used Prediction Gap Analysis to identify country-year observations where predicted GDP per capita differed from the observed value. These gaps provide useful starting points for further investigation using additional economic and country-specific information.

The key lesson from the predictive analysis is that model performance should always be interpreted in context. A high R² does not necessarily mean that the selected development indicators alone explain GDP per capita, particularly when previous-year GDP is included in the model.

Overall, the project demonstrates an end-to-end analytics workflow that moves from data preparation and validation to statistical analysis, prediction and decision-oriented interpretation.

Analytical Framework¶

Observe → Explain → Predict → Diagnose → Support Decisions

# ============================================================
# CREATE FINAL POWER BI PREDICTION DATASET
# ============================================================

powerbi_prediction = prediction_results.copy()

# Actual GDP
actual = powerbi_prediction["GDP_per_capita"]

# Linear Regression prediction
linear_pred = powerbi_prediction["Predicted_Linear"]

# Random Forest prediction
rf_pred = powerbi_prediction["Predicted_Random_Forest"]

# Calculate prediction gaps
powerbi_prediction["Linear_Gap"] = actual - linear_pred
powerbi_prediction["Linear_Absolute_Gap"] = (
    powerbi_prediction["Linear_Gap"].abs()
)

powerbi_prediction["Linear_Percentage_Error"] = (
    powerbi_prediction["Linear_Absolute_Gap"] / actual
) * 100

powerbi_prediction["Random_Forest_Gap"] = actual - rf_pred

powerbi_prediction["Random_Forest_Absolute_Gap"] = (
    powerbi_prediction["Random_Forest_Gap"].abs()
)

powerbi_prediction["Random_Forest_Percentage_Error"] = (
    powerbi_prediction["Random_Forest_Absolute_Gap"] / actual
) * 100

# Rename columns for Power BI
powerbi_prediction = powerbi_prediction.rename(columns={
    "GDP_per_capita": "Actual_GDP_per_capita",
    "Predicted_Linear": "Predicted_Linear_Regression",
    "Predicted_Random_Forest": "Predicted_Random_Forest"
})

# Keep only the columns needed for Power BI
powerbi_prediction = powerbi_prediction[
    [
        "Country_Name",
        "Country_Code",
        "Year",
        "Actual_GDP_per_capita",
        "Predicted_Linear_Regression",
        "Predicted_Random_Forest",
        "Linear_Gap",
        "Linear_Absolute_Gap",
        "Linear_Percentage_Error",
        "Random_Forest_Gap",
        "Random_Forest_Absolute_Gap",
        "Random_Forest_Percentage_Error"
    ]
]

# Export CSV
powerbi_prediction.to_csv(
    "PowerBI_Prediction_Data.csv",
    index=False
)

print("Power BI prediction dataset exported successfully.")
print(f"Rows: {len(powerbi_prediction):,}")
print("\nColumns:")
print(powerbi_prediction.columns.tolist())
